deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. Gauss builds a numerical test case: a spherical triangle ABC whose half-sums and half-differences have rational tangents, so that every trigonometric function is a square root of a rational number. He uses it to check a geometric construction behind the Gauss (Delambre–Mollweide) analogies.

1. ANGLES B, C (data). He chooses tan½(B−C)=1/2 and tan½(B+C)=3/5.
- Hence cos½(B−C)=2/√5 and sin½(B−C)=1/√5, giving ½(B−C)=26°33'54".
- cos½(B+C)=5/√34 and sin½(B+C)=3/√34, giving ½(B+C)=30°57'49".
- By the tangent addition formula: tan B=(3/5+1/2)/(1−3/10)=11/7, so cos B=7/√170, sin B=11/√170, B=57°31'43".
- tan C=(3/5−1/2)/(1+3/10)=1/13, so cos C=13/√170, sin C=1/√170, C=4°23'55".

2. SIDES b, c (data). He chooses tan½(b−c)=1/3 and tan½(b+c)=2/5.
- This choice is forced to be compatible with step 1 by Napier's analogies: tan½(b+c)/tan½(b−c)=tan½(B+C)/tan½(B−C)=6/5.
- Half-angles: ½(b−c)=18°26'6", ½(b+c)=21°48'5".
- tan b=11/13 (cos b=13/√290, sin b=11/√290), b=40°14'11".
- tan c=1/17 (cos c=17/√290, sin c=1/√290), c=3°21'59".

3. SIDE a and ANGLE A (implicit step: Napier's analogies).
- tan½a = tan½(b+c)·cos½(B+C)/cos½(B−C) = √(5/34).
- Hence cos½a=√(34/39), sin½a=√(5/39).
- Double angle: tan a=√680/29, cos a=29/39, sin a=√680/39, a=41°57'43".
- cot½A = tan½(B+C)·cos½(b+c)/cos½(b−c), so tan½A=√(29/10).
- Hence cos½A=√(10/39), sin½A=√(29/39).
- cos A=−19/39, sin A=√1160/39, tan A=−√1160/19, A=119°9'20".
- The sine rule holds: sin a/sin A = sin b/sin B = sin c/sin C = √(17/29).
- All four Gauss analogies come out as k/√39 with k=5,3,2,1.

4. THE POINT F (reconstructed from the numbers; my identification). F lies on the bisector of angle A and on the perpendicular bisector of BC, on the far side of BC from A.
- G is the midpoint of BC, with FG ⊥ CB.
- P is the foot of the perpendicular from F on CA; Q is the foot on AB extended (pencil note 'BF QF': BF=CF, QF=PF).
- The table entries are consistent with this:
  - right triangle CFG: CG=½a, angle FCG=90°−½(B+C);
  - right triangle CFP: CP=½(b−c), angle FCP=90°−½(B−C);
  - right triangle AFP: AP=½(b+c), angle FAP=½A.
- Table values:
  - CF: tan √5/3, angle 36°41'59";
  - PF: tan √(2/5), angle 32°18'41";
  - FG: tan √(125/351), angle 30°49'37";
  - AF: tan √(78/125), angle 38°18'23";
  - CFP: tan √(7/18), cos √18/5, sin √7/5;
  - CFG: tan √14/5, cos 5/√39, sin √(14/39), angle 36°48'31";
  - PFG: tan √14/44.
- A key fact, verified by the numbers: angle AFP = angle CFG (both have tan √14/5). Consequently PFG = CFG − CFP = AFB.
- At the bottom: CFB = 2·CFG, with tan √1400/11, cos 11/39, sin √1400/39, angle 73°37'2".

5. AUXILIARY TRIANGLE (lower figure).
- Each right triangle CFG and AFP is replaced by its Napier co-triangle: for CFG, legs 90°−CF and 90°−CFG, hypotenuse 90°−½a. The angles are 90°−½(B+C) at the base vertex and 90°−FG at the apex.
- Since AFP = CFG, the two co-triangles share the leg 90°−CFG and glue into one triangle:
  - sides 90°−½a, 90°−½(b+c), and base 180°−AF−CF (=104°59'38");
  - angles ½A (opposite 90°−½a), 90°−½(B+C) (opposite 90°−½(b+c)), and apex 180°−FG−FP (written 116°51'50").
- The three pairs of log sines (9.93567/9.97021, 9.93323/9.96777, 9.95040/9.98495) all differ by −0.03454/−0.03455. This verifies the sine rule in the auxiliary triangle.
- That sine rule is exactly Gauss's analogy sin½A·cos½(b+c) = cos½a·cos½(B+C).
- So the page is a numerical verification of a geometric derivation of the Gauss analogies. The next page does the companion construction with F' (on the other bisector) for the analogies involving ½(b−c).
errors: Angle CFP: Gauss writes 31°36'53", but cos CFP = √18/5 gives 31°56'53" (a 20' slip, 36 written for 56).
Propagated: PFG = CFG − CFP is written 5°11'37". With the correct CFP it is 4°51'38", which is what tan PFG = √14/44 gives. His own tangent value contradicts his degree value.
In the PFG column the cos and sin entries are swapped. They should read cos = 44/√1950 and sin = √(14/1950).
CF = 36°41'59" is about 2" too large; the exact value is 36°41'57.2".

180−FG−FP is written 116°51'50". His own FG + FP gives 116°51'42" (exact 116°51'40.6"), an 8" slip. The log sin 9.95040 follows the slipped value; the exact value is 9.95041, which fits the constant difference −0.03454 slightly better.
Minor rounding: 180−AF−CF is exactly 104°59'39.3", against 104°59'38" from his rounded AF and CF.
Otherwise all exact surd values are correct: B, C, b, c, a, A, the full CF/PF/FG/AF/CFG columns, and CFB.

results.what: Construction of a 'rational' spherical triangle (tan½(B±C), tan½(b±c) rational) consistent with Napier's analogies, so that all functions of a and A are square roots of rationals; used as a test case.
results.modern_name: Numerical test triangle via Napier's analogies / tangent half-angle parametrization
results.usually_credited_to: Napier's analogies: Napier (1614)/Briggs; the rational test-case technique is folklore

results.what: The point F where the bisector of angle A meets the perpendicular bisector of BC. It satisfies CP = BQ = ½(b−c), AP = AQ = ½(b+c), angle FCB = 90°−½(B+C), and angle AFP = angle CFG (so PFG = AFB).
results.modern_name: Spherical analogue of the arc-midpoint (South-pole) lemma; geometric proof of Mollweide/Gauss analogies
results.usually_credited_to: Plane version classical; spherical geometric proofs of the Delambre–Gauss analogies appear in 19th-century textbooks

results.what: Auxiliary spherical triangle with sides 90°−½a, 90°−½(b+c), 180°−AF−CF and angles ½A, 90°−½(B+C), 180°−FG−FP, formed by gluing the Napier co-triangles of right triangles CFG and AFP. Its sine rule gives sin½A·cos½(b+c) = cos½a·cos½(B+C), verified by logarithms.
results.modern_name: Delambre (Gauss, Mollweide) analogies; geometric derivation via associated right triangles
results.usually_credited_to: Delambre (1807), Mollweide (1808), Gauss (Theoria Motus 1809, art. 54, stated without geometric proof)

deep.surprise_reason: The analogies themselves are well known to be Gauss's (published 1809). What the page adds is a private geometric derivation, tested on a carefully designed rational triangle. This is a notable working detail of how he justified or checked them, but such geometric proofs are standard in the later literature. The page also contains arithmetic slips.

checkable.asserts: sine rule sin a/sin A = sin b/sin B holds (expect 0)
right angle at P: cos CFP = tan PF/tan CF = sqrt(18)/5
right angle at G: cos CFG = tan FG/tan CF = 5/sqrt(39)
cos CG = cos CF/cos FG = cos(a/2), so G is the midpoint of BC
tan FAP = tan PF/sin AP = tan(A/2): AF bisects angle A
tan AFP = tan AP/sin PF = sqrt(14)/5 = tan CFG

transcription_corrections: Side a: the image appears to read 41.57.43 (the exact value is 41°57'42.7"), not 41.57.40.
First line of the second block: the image has a smudged 'tg ½(b•c) = 1/3'; it is tg ½(b−c) = 1/3.
The CFP degree value 31.36.53 is faithfully transcribed, but it is Gauss's slip for 31.56.53. Likewise PFG 5.11.37 is his slip for 4.51.38.
The PFG column is faithfully transcribed as cos = √(14/1950), sin = 44/√1950; Gauss swapped these (correct: cos = 44/√1950, sin = √14/√1950).
The pencil annotation 'BF QF' above the CF and PF columns indicates BF = CF and QF = PF.
